title: 3.1.18 Functions: Definition and Calls
description: Eight multiple-choice questions on identifying calls, defining functions, hoisting, naming, and benefits. Checked instantly.

questions.question: What is wrong with this function definition's first line?
questions.explanation: A header must be function name() { — keyword, name, parentheses, brace. Indentation is a convention, not required; the keyword is correctly function, not func. The missing piece is the empty pair of parentheses after the name.

questions.question: What is the output?
options: "User info:" only — the function is never called
questions.explanation: Defining a function stores it but does not run its body. "User info:" prints first, then printPhoneNum() runs and prints the phone line.

questions.question: Which is an appropriate name for a function that calculates a user's taxes?
questions.explanation: calcTax is descriptive, camelCase, and has no spaces. "calculate user tax" has spaces, which are not legal in an identifier. cT is legal but tells a reader nothing.

questions.question: Why does this program print nothing?
options: showMenu is defined but never called
The function body is missing a return statement
questions.explanation: Defining a function only stores its code — the body never runs until something calls it. This program defines showMenu() but never calls it, so no output appears.

questions.question: This runs without error and prints "Hi!", even though the call comes before the definition. Why?
options: JavaScript scans the file first and registers function declarations before running anything — this is called hoisting
This is actually a syntax error that gets silently skipped
questions.explanation: Before running anything, JavaScript scans the whole file and registers every function declaration. By the time the first line executes, sayHello already exists.

questions.question: In the "before" version of calcDistance (math written out three times), how many lines mention a coordinate value? In the "after" version (one function, three calls)?
questions.explanation: The "before" version spends two lines per distance (declaring coordinates, then doing the math) — six lines total. The "after" version passes coordinates straight into the three calls — three lines.

questions.question: Once calcDistance() is defined, how many times can it be called?
options: As many times as you like
questions.explanation: A function definition places no limit on how many times it can be invoked. That is what reusability means.

questions.question: A repeated block of code gets moved into one function, called from three places. Which benefit does that demonstrate FIRST — before you've even called it more than once?
options: Reusability — the ability to call it again
Modularity — the task now has one name and one place it lives
Maintainability — future changes touch one spot
questions.explanation: Modularity happens the moment the task gets its own name and body, even before it's called a second time. Reusability is what you get by calling it more than once; maintainability is what you get later, when the logic needs to change.
